Introduction to Networks

Chapter 2: Configuring a Network OS

Network operating systems and the Cisco IOS CLI — console and remote access methods, IOS modes and command structure, basic device configuration and security, addressing schemes and verifying connectivity.

43 slides5 sections Full text + figures
The IOS and its functionsConsole, Telnet & SSH accessIOS modes & command structureHostnames, passwords & bannersSVI addressing & verification

★ Revision kit — Chapter 2: Configuring a Network OS

Eight structured sections for revision: overview, definitions, concept explanations, comparisons, important facts, a knowledge check, common misunderstandings and a quick revision read. Everything here is additive — the complete original slides follow below, unchanged, and every fact links back to its source slide.

From the course PDFsgrounded in the source slides (linked) Study notesupplementary wording written for this site Practicerevision questions — not lecturer or exam questions

1Chapter overviewFrom the course PDFs

Chapter 2 is about getting hands-on with the device: what a network operating system is, how the Cisco IOS CLI is reached and navigated, how to give a device an identity and lock it down (hostname, passwords, banners, encrypted password display), how configuration files are managed, and how devices are addressed — dotted-decimal IPv4 addressing, switch virtual interfaces (SVIs), automatic addressing and conflict handling — followed by connectivity testing. The chapter closes by stressing that routers and switches share the same modal, hierarchical CLI and the same initial configuration steps.

Learning objectives

  • Explain what the Cisco IOS is, where it is stored and what it lets you configure (slides 6–8).
  • Compare the CLI access methods — console, Telnet, SSH and AUX — and know when each works (slides 9–11).
  • Navigate the modal IOS hierarchy and use its help, checking and shortcut keys (slides 13–22).
  • Perform basic secure configuration: hostname, enable secret, console/VTY passwords, password encryption and banners (slides 24–30).
  • Manage configuration files and address devices — SVI configuration, automatic addressing and testing connectivity (slides 31–39).

Most important concepts

  • Cisco IOS — the collection of network operating systems on Cisco devices; the course focuses on IOS Release 15.x.
  • Modal (hierarchical) CLI — you must be in the right mode before a command works.
  • Out-of-band vs in-band access — console/AUX vs Telnet/SSH over the network.
  • Configuration files — running configuration vs startup configuration (reload / erase).
  • IPv4 dotted-decimal addressing — address + subnet mask identify a device on an internetwork.
  • SVI — a switch virtual interface gives a switch a logical (Layer 3) address.

2Key definitionsFrom the course PDFs

IOSInternetwork Operating System

The network operating system used on Cisco devices; on home routers the equivalent is usually called firmware. It provides options to configure interfaces and enable routing and switching functions. slide 6

CLICommand-Line Interface

The primary way services on Cisco IOS devices are accessed; reached via the console port, the AUX port, Telnet or SSH. slide 40

Console access

Direct connection with a special console cable; works even when no networking services are configured (out-of-band), so it should be password-protected and the device kept in a secure room. slide 10

Telnet

Remote CLI access over the network; requires active networking services and one active, configured interface. slide 11

SSHSecure Shell

Remote login similar to Telnet but with stronger password authentication and encryption when transporting data. slide 11

AUX portauxiliary port

An out-of-band connection that uses a telephone line and can be used like a console port. slide 11

Modal operating system

An OS where the technician must navigate through hierarchical modes before commands are accepted — routers and switches share this structure and many of the same commands. slide 40

enable secret

The recommended command for securing Privileged EXEC mode because it encrypts the password; the older enable password should not be used. slide 27

VTY lines

Virtual terminal lines that allow access to a device via Telnet; how many are supported varies by device and IOS version. slide 28

Banner

A message shown to all connected terminals; an important part of the legal process if someone is prosecuted for breaking in — wording implying a login is 'welcome' or 'invited' is not appropriate. slide 30

SVISwitch Virtual Interface

A logical interface on a switch (e.g. interface VLAN 1) to which an IP address and subnet mask are assigned so the switch can be managed on the network. slide 34

Dotted decimal

The structure of an IPv4 address: four decimal numbers between 0 and 255 separated by dots; used together with a subnet mask. slide 33

Subnet mask

Determined alongside the address; determines which part of a larger network is used by an IP address. slide 34

IP address conflict

Two devices configured with the same IP address — the addressing problem the chapter warns against. slide 37

Running / startup configuration

The active configuration kept in RAM versus the saved copy in NVRAM; the chapter shows saving it, reload (with 'System configuration has been modified. Save?'), erase startup-config and, on a switch, delete vlan.dat. slide 31

3Concept explanationsStudy note

Where the IOS lives and why it matters slide 7

The IOS is stored in non-volatile storage (flash) so it survives power loss, can hold multiple versions, and is copied into RAM to run. The amount of flash and RAM determines which IOS versions/feature sets a device can use.

Example: Upgrading IOS = putting a newer image in flash; the router boots by loading from flash into RAM.

Why console is 'out-of-band' slide 10

Out-of-band means the connection does not rely on the network being configured — even a device with no IP addresses at all can be reached through its console port with a console cable. Telnet and SSH are in-band: they need active networking services and one active, configured interface.

Example: A brand-new switch with no IP can still be configured by plugging a console cable into it.

Working with IOS help and shortcuts slide 21

The CLI gives context-sensitive help and syntax checking so you can discover commands as you go. Key shortcuts: Tab completes a partial command/keyword; Ctrl-A jumps to the start of the line; Ctrl-R redisplays it; Ctrl-Z exits configuration mode back to user EXEC; Ctrl-C aborts the current command; up/down arrows scroll through former commands; Ctrl-shift-6 interrupts an IOS process.

Example: Type sho then Tab — IOS completes show.

Securing access, layer by layer slide 29

Three separate protections: (1) Privileged EXEC is guarded with enable secret (encrypted — not the older enable password); (2) the console port is password-protected against physical access, and VTY lines guard remote Telnet/SSH sessions; (3) password display in the configuration is encrypted so viewers cannot read passwords — note that removing the encryption service later does not reverse existing encryption.

Example: Anyone who can read show running-config should still see only encrypted password strings, not plain text.

Giving a switch its IP address (SVI) slide 34

Switches and end devices need IPv4 addresses; addresses can be assigned to physical ports and virtual interfaces. On a switch you configure an SVI: interface VLAN 1, then ip address 192.168.10.2 255.255.255.0, then no shutdown to administratively enable the interface. Physical ports and VTY lines still need configuring for full reachability/remote management.

Example: After the SVI has an address, the switch itself can be pinged/managed from a host on that network.

Hostname rules slide 24

Naming devices matters because unnamed devices are hard to identify for configuration. The guidelines: start with a letter; no spaces; end with a letter or digit; only letters, digits and dashes; under 64 characters.

Example: Branch-SW1 fits every rule; branch sw 1 breaks three of them.

Technical terms are kept exactly as the course uses them; the plain-language wording and examples are supplementary study notes.

4ComparisonsFrom the course PDFs

Console vs Telnet/SSH (access methods)

AspectConsoleTelnet / SSH
BandOut-of-band — no networking services requiredIn-band — over the network
PrerequisitesSpecial console cable; device reachable even unconfiguredActive networking services and one active, configured interface
Typical useInitial configuration; rescue when network is downDay-to-day remote management
Security notePhysically secure the device/roomSSH preferred: authentication + encryption

AUX is also out-of-band (telephone line), used like a console port. slide 9 slide 10 slide 11

Telnet vs SSH

AspectTelnetSSH
PurposeRemote CLI login over the networkRemote CLI login over the network
SecurityNo encryption of transported data mentioned — basic remote loginStronger password authentication
Data protectionData sent in clear as far as the chapter's contrast impliesUses encryption when transporting data
Chapter verdictOlder methodSimilar to Telnet, but more secure

Both require active networking services and a configured interface. slide 11

5Important factsFrom the course PDFs

  • The course's primary focus is Cisco IOS Release 15.x; every networking device comes with a default IOS that can be upgraded (version or feature set). slide 6
  • IOS is kept in non-volatile storage (flash) and copied to RAM to run; flash/RAM quantity determines usable IOS. slide 7
  • CLI access methods: Console, Telnet or SSH, AUX. slide 9
  • Terminal emulation programs named: PuTTY, Tera Term, SecureCRT, HyperTerminal, OS X Terminal. slide 12
  • Shortcut keys: Tab (complete), Ctrl-R (redisplay), Ctrl-A (line start), Ctrl-Z (exit config mode), Ctrl-C (abort), arrows (command history), Ctrl-shift-6 (interrupt process). slide 21
  • show version displays the IOS version and related device information. slide 22
  • Hostname rules: starts with a letter, no spaces, ends with letter/digit, only letters/digits/dashes, fewer than 64 characters. slide 24
  • Use enable secret, not enable password — enable secret provides greater security because the password is encrypted. slide 27
  • Console must be secured (physical plug-in risk); VTY lines allow Telnet access; count varies by device/IOS version. slide 28
  • Password encryption in the configuration is one-way: removing the encryption service does not reverse the encryption. slide 29
  • Config file operations: reload asks 'System configuration has been modified. Save? [yes/no]'; erase startup-config removes the startup config; switches also need delete vlan.dat. slide 31
  • IPv4 addresses are dotted decimal — four numbers 0–255 — and are always used with a subnet mask; addresses can go on physical ports and virtual interfaces. slide 33
  • SVI configuration pattern: interface VLAN 1 → ip address 192.168.10.2 255.255.255.0 → no shutdown (administratively enables the interface). slide 34
  • Routers and switches share the same modal operating system structure, command structures and many commands, with identical initial configuration steps. slide 40

6Knowledge checkPractice

8 practice questions — a mix of multiple-choice, true/false, short-answer and explanation tasks. Answers stay hidden until you reveal them, and each one explains why it is correct. These are revision questions written for this site from the course content — they are not lecturer instructions or examination questions.

Multiple choiceQ1. Which CLI access method works even when the device has no networking services configured?

  • A. Telnet
  • B. SSH
  • C. Console
  • D. AUX over IP
Show answer & explanation

Answer: C — Console

Why: Console access is out-of-band: the device is accessible even if no networking services have been configured, using a special console cable (slide 10).

True or falseQ2. For securing Privileged EXEC access mode, the chapter says to use the older enable password command rather than enable secret.

Show answer & explanation

Answer: False

Why: The opposite: use enable secret, not the older enable password, because enable secret provides greater security — the password is encrypted (slide 27).

Short answerQ3. List the hostname guidelines given in the chapter (any four).

Show answer & explanation

Answer: Start with a letter; contain no spaces; end with a letter or digit; use only letters, digits and dashes; be less than 64 characters long.

Why: Slide 24 lists exactly these — and notes that devices without names are difficult to identify for configuration purposes.

Multiple choiceQ4. What does the no shutdown command do in the SVI configuration?

  • A. Saves the running configuration
  • B. Administratively enables the interface
  • C. Restarts the switch
  • D. Encrypts all passwords
Show answer & explanation

Answer: B — Administratively enables the interface

Why: Slide 34: after ip address …, no shutdown administratively enables the interface (the switch still needs physical ports configured and VTY lines for remote management).

Short answerQ5. Where is the IOS stored, and where does it run from?

Show answer & explanation

Answer: Stored in non-volatile storage (flash); copied into volatile RAM to run. Flash and RAM sizes determine which IOS can be used.

Why: Slide 7: non-volatile storage keeps it when power is lost; it can hold multiple versions and is copied from flash to RAM.

ExplanationQ6. Explain why the banner message matters legally, and what kind of wording is inappropriate.

Show answer & explanation

Answer: The banner is displayed to all connected terminals and is an important part of the legal process if someone is prosecuted for breaking into the device. Wording that implies a login is 'welcome' or 'invited' is not appropriate.

Why: Slide 30 states both points directly.

True or falseQ7. SSH provides stronger password authentication and encrypts data in transit, while Telnet does not encrypt the transported data.

Show answer & explanation

Answer: True

Why: Slide 11: SSH is 'similar to Telnet, but utilizes more security — stronger password authentication, uses encryption when transporting data'.

ExplanationQ8. A student runs the command that disables the encryption service after seeing encrypted passwords in running-config, expecting the plain-text passwords to come back. Why is this wrong?

Show answer & explanation

Answer: Because once applied, removing the encryption service does not reverse the encryption — the stored passwords remain encrypted.

Why: Slide 29 states this explicitly; the encryption of existing entries is one-way.

7Common misunderstandingsStudy note

<code>enable password</code> vs <code>enable secret</code>

Both guard Privileged EXEC, but only enable secret encrypts the password. The chapter explicitly says to use enable secret and avoid the older enable password (slide 27).

"Remote access works without configuration"

Telnet/SSH are in-band: they need active networking services and an active, configured interface. Only console/AUX are out-of-band and available on an unconfigured device (slides 10–11).

Turning off password encryption reveals plain-text passwords

No — removing the encryption service does not reverse encryption already applied; passwords stay encrypted (slide 29).

Configuring only the SVI is enough for a switch

The SVI gives the switch an address, but the chapter notes the switch still needs physical ports configured and VTY lines set to enable remote management (slide 34).

8Quick revision (2–5 minutes)Study note

  • IOS: network OS for Cisco devices (focus: Release 15.x); stored in flash, runs from RAM; configure interfaces, enable routing/switching.
  • Reach the CLI: console (out-of-band, works unconfigured), Telnet/SSH (in-band, need configured interface; SSH = stronger auth + encryption), AUX (telephone line, out-of-band). Tools: PuTTY, Tera Term, SecureCRT, HyperTerminal.
  • Modes: modal, hierarchical — routers and switches share the same structure and initial configuration steps; context-sensitive help, syntax check, Tab/arrow shortcuts; show version for versions.
  • Basic config: hostname (letter start, no spaces, letters/digits/dashes, <64 chars) → secure with enable secret (not enable password), console password, VTY passwords, encrypt password display (irreversible), set a legal banner (never 'welcome').
  • Config files: save before reload; erase startup-config (+ delete vlan.dat on switches) clears saved config.
  • Addressing: IPv4 = dotted decimal (4 × 0–255) + subnet mask; switch gets an IP via SVI: interface VLAN 1 → ip address … → no shutdown; avoid address conflicts; test connectivity.

The Command Structure

Hot Keys and Shortcuts

  • Tab – Completes the remainder of a partially typed command or keyword.
  • Ctrl-R – Redisplays a line.
  • Ctrl-A – Moves to the beginning of the line.
  • Ctrl-Z – Exits the configuration mode and returns to user EXEC.
  • Down Arrow – Allows the user to scroll forward through former commands.
  • Up Arrow – Allows the user to scroll backward through former commands.
  • Ctrl-shift-6 – Allows the user to interrupt an IOS process such

as ping or traceroute.

  • Ctrl-C – Exits the current configuration or aborts the current command.

Hostnames

Device Names

Some guidelines for naming conventions:

  • Start with a letter
  • Contains no spaces
  • Ends with a letter or digit
  • Uses only letters, digits, and dashes
  • Be less than 64 characters in length

Without names, network

devices are difficult to

identify for configuration

purposes.

Slide 33
Ports and Addresses

IP Addressing of Devices

  • Each end device on a network must be configured with an IP address.
  • Structure of an IPv4 address is called dotted decimal.
  • IP address displayed in decimal notation, with four decimal numbers between 0 and 255.
  • With the IP address, a subnet mask is also necessary.
  • IP addresses can be assigned to both physical ports and virtual interfaces.

Chapter 2 Summary

3 slides
Slide 40
Configuring a Network Operating System

Chapter 2 Summary

Cisco IOS:

The technician can enter commands to configure, or program, the

device to perform various networking functions.

Services are generally accessed using a command-line interface

(CLI), which is accessed by either the console port, the AUX port, or

through telnet or SSH.

Once connected to the CLI, network technicians can make

configuration changes to Cisco IOS devices.

Cisco IOS is designed as a modal operating system, which means a

network technician must navigate through various hierarchical

modes of the IOS.

Cisco IOS routers and switches support a similar modal operating

system, support similar command structures, and support many of

the same commands. In addition, both devices have identical initial

configuration steps when implementing them in a network.
